issues.legal_issue: A later transfer of a right to repurchase was not defeated by an earlier purported transfer that the lower courts found to be sham and ineffective.
material_facts: The original landowner first purported to transfer the repurchase right to other purchasers and later transferred it to the plaintiffs.
The lower appellate court found the earlier transfer sham, found that it conveyed no title, and relied also on evidence that the earlier purchasers had surrendered any interest.
The High Court affirmed those factual findings, and the matter reached the Supreme Court by appeal by special leave.
issues.conclusion: The earlier purported transfer did not defeat the plaintiffs’ right, and the challenge to their claim failed. The Supreme Court would not go behind the concurrent factual findings in an appeal by special leave.
issues.legal_principle: In an appeal by special leave under Article 136, the Supreme Court would not go behind the lower courts’ findings of fact. No earlier cases were relied on.

predicates.special_leave_appeal: The matter is brought to the Supreme Court by appeal after special leave is granted.
predicates.lower_courts_found_earlier_transfer_sham: The lower courts found that an earlier purported transfer of the right was a sham transaction.
predicates.earlier_transferees_acquired_no_title: The lower courts found that the persons named in the earlier transfer acquired no title to the right.

issues.definition: When an appeal by special leave challenges a later assignment after the lower courts found an earlier purported transfer sham and ineffective, the later assignment is not defeated on that ground.

issues.legal_issue: The statutory restriction on a land transfer did not apply unless the transferee’s resulting aggregate landholding exceeded the applicable ceiling.
material_facts: The appellant argued that the transfer was invalid because the plaintiffs’ landholdings exceeded the statutory ceiling.
The District Judge found that the plaintiffs’ landholdings did not exceed the applicable ceiling, and the High Court affirmed that finding.
The appellant had not produced landholding records establishing that the plaintiffs would exceed the ceiling as a result of the transfer.
issues.conclusion: The plaintiffs’ landholdings did not exceed the applicable ceiling, so the restriction did not apply and the appellant’s contention failed.
issues.legal_principle: Section 154 of the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950 applied only if the transferee would, as a result of the transfer, hold land in aggregate exceeding the applicable ceiling. The Court noted the ceiling was 12½ acres under the provision as set out and had been increased to 30 acres at the relevant period. No earlier cases were relied on.

predicates.specific_performance_suit: The proceeding seeks specific performance of an agreement to transfer land.
predicates.land_transfer_subject_to_holding_restric: The proposed land transfer is subject to a restriction based on the transferee’s aggregate landholding.
predicates.transferee_resulting_holding_below_appli: The transferee’s aggregate landholding after the transfer does not exceed the applicable ceiling.

issues.definition: In a suit for specific performance involving a land transfer subject to a holding restriction, the restriction is not triggered when the transferee’s resulting aggregate holding is within the applicable ceiling.
